problems: stop 1 card 2, answer 1: copies a Prep line word for word

explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "Stand firm, then" right after, "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free" (Galatians 5:1). Christ already unlocked the chains; their job is not to crawl back to the cell. Standing firm means holding onto what Jesus did, even when people try to pile rules on your shoulders again.

explanations.answer: Work hard to earn their freedom
explanations.explanation: Not this one. Paul says Christ HAS set them free already; he does not tell them to earn it by working harder (Galatians 5:1). Freedom is a gift from Jesus, not a prize for performance. Their job is to stand firm in what He’s done, not try to buy it back with effort.

No silence here, friend. Paul says, "Stand firm" and "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). He’s warning them against going backward into law-slavery, not telling them to hide what Christ has done. This is about guarding freedom, not tiptoeing with it.

Yes. Paul warns them "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" right after saying Christ set them free (Galatians 5:1). That yoke is going back under the law as the way to be right with God. He wants them living in the freedom Jesus gave, not carrying those old chains again.

Paul really does give this warning. He says, "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). That means there’s a real danger of going backwards into law-slavery if they listen to the wrong teaching. His whole point is to keep them standing in Christ’s freedom, not under that yoke again.

That’s what Paul says, and he signs it with his own name. "I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). If they choose law as their way to be right with God, they’re walking away from Christ as their way. You can’t hold on to both as your foundation.

Paul says the opposite. He warns, "if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). The moment they make law-keeping their way of being right with God, they’re not trusting Christ anymore. That doesn’t add to Christ’s value; it throws it away.

Paul doesn’t say Christ’s value stays the same if they go this route. He says, "if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). Trusting law as the way to be justified pushes Jesus out of that place. It’s a switch of foundations, not a little adjustment.

Paul actually says much more than that. He warns, "every man who gets himself circumcised… is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). If you choose the law system, you sign up for the entire thing, not just one command. It’s all-or-nothing, and that’s Paul’s point.

Right, Paul does NOT limit it to one command. He says, "every man who gets himself circumcised… is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). If they choose law as their way to be right with God, they are on the hook for every part of it. That’s why he’s warning them so sharply.

explanations.answer: They have been severed from Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes, and Paul does not soften it. He says, "You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). Trying to be justified that way cuts them off from Christ as their righteousness. Grace and law-as-ladder don’t share the same throne.

explanations.answer: They have drawn closer to Christ
explanations.explanation: Paul says the exact opposite. He writes, "You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). Leaning on law as the way to be right with God doesn’t bring them closer; it cuts them off from trusting Christ. It swaps grace out for self-effort.

No bonus points here, baker. Paul says those who try to be justified by the law "have been severed from Christ" and "have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). That means you can’t stack grace on top of law-earning. When you choose law as your ladder, you step off grace entirely.

Exactly. Paul says, "by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). Faith is the way they wait, trusting what Christ has done and what He will finish. The Spirit keeps that hope alive, not their law performance.

Paul doesn’t say they wait by law. He writes, "by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). The waiting is full of trust in what Christ has done, not pressure to keep the rules perfectly. The Spirit, not the law, carries that hope in them.

Paul doesn’t point to their effort here. He says, "by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). Effort has its place, but the foundation of their hope is trusting Christ, not grinding harder. It’s faith, carried by the Spirit, that looks ahead to full righteousness.

Yes, that’s Paul’s bottom line in this section. He says, "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). The big question is not, "What mark do you have?" but, "Are you trusting Christ, and is that trust showing up in love?" That’s the kind of faith that fits life in Him.

Paul doesn’t put that at the center here. He says, "neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value" and then, "What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). He’s moving them away from a checklist mindset. The real mark is faith in Christ that shows itself by loving others.

explanations.answer: Coming from the right family line
explanations.explanation: Lineage is not Paul’s focus at all in this verse. He says, "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value" (Galatians 5:6). Then he nails it: "What matters is faith expressing itself through love." In Christ, it’s not about which family you’re from, but whether you trust Him and let that trust spill out in love.

Paul actually says that persuasion does NOT come from the One who calls them. In Galatians 5:8 he writes, "Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you." The pressure that’s slowing them down is not from God. That’s why he’s so serious about it.

Right. Paul says, "Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you" (Galatians 5:8). The voice pushing them back toward law-slavery is not the Lord’s voice. That warning helps them test where a teaching really comes from.

You got it, baker. Paul says, "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). Just a little false teaching can spread through a whole church if nobody deals with it. That’s why he doesn’t treat this like a tiny side issue.

Paul paints a bigger picture than that. He says, "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). In his image, the influence doesn’t stay on the surface; it spreads everywhere. He wants them to see how serious a “little” error can be.

Paul is warning that it spreads much farther than one spot. He says, "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). That means this wrong teaching about the law won’t stay contained. Left alone, it moves through the whole community.

Yes. Paul says, "The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). He’s confident in the Lord that the Galatians will come back to the right view, and he’s sure God will deal with the troublemaker. Nobody gets to lead people astray for free.

explanations.answer: He will be let off free
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn’t talk about the man getting off easy. He says, "The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). That means this person is accountable before God for the confusion he’s caused. Paul is trusting the Lord to handle that justice.

explanations.answer: He will be put in charge
explanations.explanation: Oh no, friend, Paul is not recommending a promotion. He writes, "The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). This person is facing judgment, not leadership. Paul is confident the Lord will sort that out.

If Paul were still preaching circumcision, his suffering wouldn’t make sense, and he says that to make a point. In Galatians 5:11 he asks, "If I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?" He’s not admitting he still preaches it; he’s showing that his persecution proves he doesn’t. The message of the cross is what’s getting him in trouble.

Correct. Paul uses a question to show the opposite. He says, "If I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?" (Galatians 5:11). His point is that the persecution proves he’s not preaching circumcision anymore. It’s the offense of the cross that is still very much alive in his message.

Yes. Paul tells them, "you… were called to freedom" and right away adds, "but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13). Freedom in Christ isn’t a permission slip to indulge sinful desires. Instead, he calls them to use that freedom to "serve one another in love."

Paul really does give this warning. He writes, "you… were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13). He doesn’t want them swinging from law-slavery to selfish living. The right use of freedom is to "serve one another in love."

Yes, that’s the line Paul highlights. He says, "The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'" (Galatians 5:14). Loving others from the heart sums up what the law was aiming at. It’s the kind of love that flows from faith in Christ.

Paul doesn’t pick that command here. He says, "The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'" (Galatians 5:14). Remembering the Sabbath is important in the law, but this verse is zooming in on love for your neighbor as the summary. That’s the one that gathers the rest up.

Honoring parents is part of God’s law, but it’s not the single decree Paul names in this verse. He writes, "The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'" (Galatians 5:14). That command covers how we treat every neighbor, including family. It’s the big umbrella he points to.

Yes. Paul warns, "if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). That picture is about a community tearing itself apart from the inside. It’s the opposite of that "serve one another in love" he just called them to.

Paul uses a stronger word here. He says, "if you keep on biting and devouring one another… you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). This isn’t just about people getting spread out; it’s about them destroying each other. That’s why he’s calling them back to love.

Shame might come with that kind of fighting, but Paul’s word goes even further. He warns they will be "consumed by one another" if they keep biting and devouring (Galatians 5:15). It’s a picture of mutual destruction, not just embarrassment. He wants them to see how serious their conflicts can become.
